strengths: Originality: Combining a pretrained tabular PFN with per-feature graph attention adapters and a graph-aware synthetic prior is a useful methodological contribution. The combination of overlapping stochastic block structures, preferential attachment, and graph-dependent SCM attributes provides a plausible approach to synthetic graph pretraining.

Significance: Finetuning produces meaningful improvements over strong baselines. Table 2 reports 53.08 versus 49.88 on artnet-exp, 79.15 versus 76.32 on hm-prices, and 64.15 versus 62.12 on artnet-views compared with finetuned G2T-LimiX.

Soundness: Evaluation includes classification and regression across diverse graph domains, strengthened conventional GNN baselines, and ten repeated runs. Appendix B provides a valuable architecture-matched comparison: pretrained adapters consistently outperform randomly initialized adapters, supporting the usefulness of pretraining.

Presentation and limitations: The architectural explanation and Figure 1 clearly distinguish global PFN attention from local graph attention. Appendix A candidly discusses scalability, prior coverage, limited ablations, and task restrictions. No material research-ethics concern is apparent from the described benchmark experiments.
weaknesses: Reproducibility is inadequate for the central contribution. Section 4 says that prior hyperparameters are sampled from distributions but does not specify those distributions, including graph sizes, block counts, degree sequences, or preferential-attachment parameters. The graph SCM also lacks the GNN operator and LapPE sampling details. These choices define the training distribution and cannot be reconstructed reliably from the conceptual description. Despite claiming public availability, the manuscript supplies no identifiable code or checkpoint link.

The strongest results depend on an unspecified finetuning protocol. Section 5 refers readers to Appendix D, but that appendix only describes PCA preprocessing. Finetuning learning rates, training duration, context/query construction, checkpoint selection, baseline search spaces, and tuning budgets are absent. It is also unclear whether the ten runs vary splits or only random seeds. Consequently, the fairness and reproducibility of the headline comparisons cannot be assessed.

Soundness of the prior-design claims remains insufficiently established. Appendix B demonstrates the benefit of the complete pretraining procedure, but does not isolate the proposed structural prior, graph-aware SCM, or masked graph modeling objective. There is no simpler-prior comparison or quantitative comparison of synthetic and real graph statistics; visual examples alone do not establish realism. The acknowledged computational constraints explain the limited ablation but leave the specific methodological claims unverified.

The training description does not adequately explain regression, despite regression accounting for several headline gains. Section 3.2 specifies cross-entropy for the supervised PFN objective without describing target discretization, a regression head, or prediction decoding. The synthetic-target construction likewise does not explain how classification and regression tasks are formed.

Significance is narrower than the broad performance claims suggest. In-context GraphPFN substantially trails G2T-LimiX on several datasets, including hm-prices, avazu-ctr, and twitch-views, while finetuning runs out of memory on four of thirteen datasets, including the 19,717-node pubmed graph. No downstream runtime or memory measurements quantify these tradeoffs. Observation 2 also claims seven wins among ten successfully finetuned datasets, whereas Tables 2–3 show only nine successful datasets; some small reported wins, such as questions, are not clearly resolved by the reported variability. These issues require more precise claims and stronger experimental documentation before acceptance.

strengths: Originality: Combining graph attention adapters in a pretrained tabular PFN with a synthetic attributed-graph prior is a useful methodological contribution. The overlapping SBM construction, preferential attachment, and graph-aware SCM provide a coherent approach to synthetic graph pretraining.

Significance: Finetuning produces meaningful improvements over strong reported baselines. For example, GraphPFN improves hm-prices from 76.32 to 79.15 and artnet-exp from 49.88 to 53.08 relative to finetuned G2T-LimiX (Table 2). Evaluation covers classification and regression, heterogeneous feature types, and both homophilous and heterophilous graphs.

Soundness: The architecture-matched random-adapter comparison in Table 4 supports the value of synthetic pretraining: pretrained adapters outperform randomly initialized adapters on all nine evaluated datasets. Reporting means and standard deviations over ten runs is also helpful.

Presentation and limitations: The architecture and motivation are clearly explained. Appendix A candidly identifies scalability, prior coverage, class-count restrictions, and limited ablations. These disclosures are appropriate; no material research-ethics concern is apparent from the manuscript.
weaknesses: Reproducibility is materially inadequate for the central contribution. Section 4 says graph-generator hyperparameters follow sampled distributions but does not specify those distributions, including block sizes, degree sequences, and preferential-attachment settings. The graph-aware SCM also omits its GNN operator and several sampling details. Without these specifications, the proposed prior cannot be faithfully reconstructed. Despite claiming public availability, the manuscript provides no code or checkpoint access location.

The downstream protocol is substantially underspecified. Section 5 refers readers to Appendix D, but that appendix only discusses PCA. Finetuning learning rates, training duration, stopping rules, label/context masking, hyperparameter search spaces and budgets, and the source of variation across ten runs are not documented. Section 3.2 describes only a cross-entropy supervised objective, leaving the implementation of the reported regression tasks unexplained. These omissions prevent reliable reproduction and assessment of comparison fairness.

The evidence does not establish the importance of the proposed prior design. Table 4 tests pretraining as a whole, but there are no comparisons with simpler graph priors or ablations of overlapping SBMs, preferential attachment, graph-aware SCM components, or the masked graph modeling objective. The claimed realism of the prior is supported mainly by visualizations, without quantitative comparisons to real graph statistics. Thus, the distinctive prior mechanisms remain insufficiently validated.

The broad generalization claims exceed the evidence. In-context GraphPFN substantially trails G2T-LimiX on several datasets: without LapPE, hm-prices is 68.02 versus 74.96, avazu-ctr is 21.67 versus 32.39, and twitch-views is 59.95 versus 71.08. Finetuning runs out of memory on four of thirteen datasets, including pubmed with only 19,717 nodes. No downstream runtime or peak-memory comparison establishes the practical tradeoff. These results support useful gains on selected tasks, but not uniformly strong graph-foundation-model performance.

Presentation contains a concrete evaluation inconsistency: Section 5.2 claims successful finetuning on ten datasets, whereas Tables 2–3 show only nine, consistent with Table 4. The claimed seven wins also combine results with and without LapPE; a validation-based rule for selecting these variants is not specified. Overall, the promising empirical results do not outweigh the missing methodological specifications and insufficient evidence for the central prior-design claims.

The combination of overlapping stochastic block structures, preferential attachment, and graph-dependent SCMs provides a plausible approach to synthetic graph pretraining.

Significance: Finetuning produces meaningful improvements over strong baselines. For example, GraphPFN achieves 53.08 versus 49.88 on artnet-exp, 79.15 versus 76.32 on hm-prices, and 64.15 versus 62.12 on artnet-views compared with finetuned G2T-LimiX. Evaluation covers heterogeneous domains, classification and regression, and both homophilous and heterophilous graphs.

Soundness: Table 4 provides a valuable architecture-matched control: pretrained adapters outperform randomly initialized adapters on all nine reported datasets. This supports the importance of synthetic pretraining beyond simply adding model capacity. Reporting ten runs and including strengthened classic GNN baselines are also positives.

Presentation and limitations: The architectural description and Figure 1 clearly explain the interaction between global PFN attention and local graph attention. Appendix A candidly acknowledges scalability, prior coverage, and task limitations. No material research-ethics concern is evident from the described work.
weaknesses: Reproducibility is materially inadequate. Section 4 does not specify the distributions and ranges defining the proposed graph prior, including SBM parameters, preferential-attachment degrees, and several attribute-generation choices. Downstream finetuning schedules, context construction, hyperparameter search spaces, and model-selection procedures are also absent. Appendix D supplies only a short PCA discussion, despite being referenced for experimental details. The manuscript claims public availability but provides no code or checkpoint link.

Soundness: The training description specifies cross-entropy for node prediction, but several central results concern regression. The manuscript does not explain the regression output representation, objective, or how synthetic targets become classification or regression tasks. This leaves a substantial part of the reported evaluation methodologically unspecified.

Evidence for the distinctive prior is insufficient. Table 4 establishes the benefit of pretraining the adapters, but does not isolate the proposed multi-SBM construction, preferential attachment, graph-aware SCM, or MGM objective. No simpler-prior comparison or quantitative synthetic-versus-real graph analysis is provided; graph visualizations alone do not establish realism. The acknowledged computational constraints explain the missing ablations but do not substantiate the central attribution to a well-designed prior.

Significance is narrower than the broad performance claims suggest. ICL performance has substantial deficits, including 68.02 versus 74.96 on hm-prices and 21.67 versus 32.39 on avazu-ctr relative to G2T-LimiX. Finetuning fails with OOM on four of thirteen datasets, including pubmed with only 19,717 nodes. Thus, applicability depends on more than node count, and inference/finetuning memory and runtime comparisons are needed to assess practical usefulness.

Presentation and evaluation precision need improvement. Observation 2 reports seven wins among ten successfully finetuned datasets, whereas Tables 2–4 show nine successful datasets. Several winning margins are small relative to reported variability, and the paper does not explain how the variants with and without LapPE are selected. The concluding claim of consistently achieving state-of-the-art results should be qualified. Overall, the promising empirical gains do not yet outweigh the missing methodological specifications and evidence needed to reproduce and attribute them.

strengths: Originality: GraphPFN offers a useful extension of tabular PFNs through graph attention adapters and synthetic graph pretraining. The combination of multilevel SBMs, preferential attachment, and graph-aware SCMs is a substantive methodological contribution.

Significance: Evaluation covers 13 datasets spanning classification, regression, tabular features, and text-derived features. Finetuned, ensembled GraphPFN achieves the highest reported mean on 10 datasets, with substantial improvements over G2T-LimiX on artnet-views, hm-prices, and twitch-views.

Soundness: Comparisons include strong backbone-matched PFN baselines and improved classic GNNs, with results reported over ten runs. Table 6 supports the importance of graph pretraining beyond simply adding adapters; Table 5 provides useful comparisons with simpler structural priors.

Presentation and limitations: The architecture and training stages are clearly explained. Appendix A candidly identifies scalability, domain coverage, class-count, and task restrictions. No material research-ethics concern is apparent.
weaknesses: Reproducibility is the decisive weakness. Section 4.1 does not specify the probability distributions governing SBM blocks, degree sequences, graph composition, or preferential attachment, although these distributions define the central proposed prior. Context-size sampling and several attribute-generation choices are also unspecified. The abstract's code-availability statement supplies no link.

The strongest results depend on full finetuning, but its learning rates, optimization budget, context/query construction, and label-masking procedure are not documented. Likewise, the claimed extensive GNN tuning lacks search spaces and budgets. References to earlier protocols do not fully specify these graph-specific experiments.

The ablations establish that pretraining helps, but do not isolate the contribution of graph-aware attribute generation, multilevel SBM composition versus preferential attachment, masked graph modeling, or added random features. Table 5 evaluates structural alternatives only after Stage 1 and provides no uncertainty estimates, limiting conclusions about why the complete method works.

Generalization evidence is restricted to random 10%/10%/80% transductive splits. Different label budgets and inductive or distribution-shift evaluations would better substantiate the broader foundation-model claims. The reported ten-run deviations are not clearly distinguished as variation across splits versus model randomness.

Practical efficiency remains unquantified: avoiding graph-feature preprocessing does not establish lower total cost without inference latency, finetuning time, and peak-memory comparisons. Appendix D reports a finetuning OOM on pubmed, yet Table 2 places substituted ICL results in FT rows without a table-level marker.

The prior-realism analysis is limited to marginal summary statistics and visual examples; it does not establish realistic joint structure–attribute relationships. Consequently, the promising benchmark gains support the approach more strongly than the broader claims about a realistic prior and generalizable graph modeling.

strengths: Originality: The combination of graph-aware synthetic pretraining, a multi-level SBM/preferential-attachment prior, and graph-dependent SCM attributes is a useful extension of tabular PFNs. The contribution goes beyond applying an existing tabular model to engineered graph features.

Significance: Evaluation covers 13 datasets, classification and regression, and both tabular and text-derived features. GraphPFN with finetuning and ensembling wins on 10 datasets, with meaningful improvements over G2T-LimiX on artnet-views, hm-prices, and twitch-views (Tables 1–2).

Soundness: The comparisons include strong same-backbone PFN baselines and enhanced conventional GNNs. Table 6 controls for architecture by finetuning randomly initialized graph adapters and shows substantial degradation, providing credible evidence that graph pretraining contributes to performance. Table 5 also supports the proposed structural prior against simpler generators.

Presentation and limitations: The architecture and transductive information flow are explained clearly. Appendix A appropriately acknowledges memory demands, prior mismatch, class-count restrictions, and the restriction to node-level tasks. No material research-ethics concern is apparent from the described work.
weaknesses: Reproducibility is the decisive concern. Section 4.1 says that distributions are defined for the graph generator's many hyperparameters but does not provide those distributions, including block counts, sizes, degree sequences, and preferential-attachment parameters. These choices define the central contribution—the training prior—and cannot be recovered from the conceptual description. The abstract's code-availability sentence contains no link in the supplied manuscript.

The downstream protocol is insufficiently specified. Appendix D provides PCA and ensembling details but omits concrete finetuning learning rates, training budgets, optimizer settings, context/query construction during optimization, and early-stopping settings. The claimed extensive GNN hyperparameter tuning is also not accompanied by search spaces or budgets. It is unclear whether the ten repetitions vary data splits or only execution randomness. These omissions make the reported comparisons difficult to reproduce and audit.

The ablations support the overall approach more strongly than its individual design claims. Table 5 tests only first-stage structural-generator substitutions, without uncertainty estimates; there are no corresponding controls for graph-aware SCM attributes, Laplacian inputs, or the masked graph modeling objective. Consequently, the contribution of several prominently motivated components remains unresolved.

Practical significance is not adequately quantified. Avoiding positional-encoding preprocessing is useful, but there are no downstream runtime or peak-memory comparisons, including the cost of ten-member ensembling. Appendix D reports that finetuning runs out of memory on pubmed and requires PCA on two other datasets. These limitations are honestly disclosed, but resource measurements are needed to establish the method's practical tradeoffs.

Some presentation and generalization claims need qualification. Table 2 places unchanged pubmed ICL results in rows labeled FT, with the exception explained only in Appendix D; it should be marked directly in the table. More broadly, evaluation uses a single 10%/10%/80% random-split regime, so robustness across label budgets and distribution shifts remains untested. The evidence establishes promising performance within the evaluated setting, rather than broad graph-foundation-model generality.

strengths: Originality: GraphPFN offers a meaningful extension of tabular PFNs to graphs through graph-specific synthetic pretraining and per-feature neighborhood-attention adapters. The combination of multi-level SBMs, preferential attachment, and graph-aware attribute generation is a useful methodological contribution.

Significance: The evaluation covers 13 datasets spanning classification, regression, tabular and text-derived features, and different homophily regimes. Finetuned, ensembled GraphPFN wins on 10 datasets, with substantial improvements over G2T-LimiX on artnet-views, hm-prices, and twitch-views.

Soundness: Comparisons include relevant PFN-based competitors and strengthened conventional GNNs, with results reported over 10 runs. Table 6 provides particularly useful evidence: the same architecture with randomly initialized adapters performs substantially worse, supporting the contribution of graph pretraining beyond architecture alone.
The simpler-prior comparisons in Table 5 support the proposed generator: it achieves the best first-stage performance on six of eight datasets under a matched training stage.

Presentation is generally clear, especially the explanation of global PFN attention versus local graph attention. Appendix A candidly identifies scalability, prior coverage, class-count, and task limitations. No material research-ethics concern is apparent from the described experiments.
weaknesses: Reproducibility is the decisive weakness. Section 4.1 says graph-generator hyperparameters are sampled from distributions but never specifies those distributions, including block counts and sizes, degree parameters, and the preferential-attachment allocation. These choices define the central prior and cannot be reconstructed from the qualitative description. The manuscript also leaves the advertised code location blank.

The downstream protocol is insufficiently specified despite the strongest claims depending on finetuning. Section 5 and Appendix D omit concrete finetuning learning rates, optimization budgets, context/query construction during training, and early-stopping settings. The claimed extensive GNN tuning lacks search spaces and budgets. It is also unclear whether the 10 runs vary data splits or only model randomness, limiting interpretation of the reported uncertainty.

Component attribution remains incomplete. Table 6 establishes the value of pretrained adapters, but there are no controlled ablations for graph-aware attribute generation, the masked-graph objective, or added random features. Table 5 compares whole structure generators only after stage 1 and reports no uncertainty, so it does not isolate the benefits of the individual proposed structural components.

The evidence supports performance on the selected transductive node tasks more strongly than broad graph-foundation-model generality. All experiments use one label fraction, and no inductive or alternative-split evaluation is provided. The prior-realism analysis compares marginal summary statistics; it does not establish joint structural fidelity, and Table 4 misses important properties of city-roads-M and twitch-views. These are limits on the demonstrated reach, rather than objections to the honest limitations discussion.

Practical cost remains difficult to assess. Pretraining requires approximately 1,344 A100 GPU-hours, but inference latency, finetuning cost, and peak memory are not compared with competitors. Appendix D reports PCA interventions and an out-of-memory failure on pubmed; nevertheless, Table 2 places pubmed ICL results in rows labeled FT without a table-level caveat. Clearer labeling and resource measurements are needed to assess the claimed practical advantages.
